comments.author: kingmob
comments.text:
As a long-term Warp user, this makes me hopeful. I started using it well before the rise in AI, because Warp offered excellent performance, but more importantly, a rethink of what the terminal should look like in the 21st c.

Warp turns the terminal into more of a REPL/chat, and less of a grid of characters. There's a permanent input box at the bottom, with lots of little metadata that usually shows up in your $PS1. The input behaves like the rest of your OS inputs, leveraging muscle memory.

Each command adds to a growing stack of cells above with command+output. You can copy a whole cell, or just its output with a right-click, without highlighting the exact output. You can search just a single cell's contents. (It still falls back to a fullscreen grid of chars when needed, depending on the command.) Ctrl+R pops up a GUI history search.

I wouldn't say it's been 100% smooth. The way the input works interferes with custom keybindings. And I have no strong opinion on Warp's collaboration features or AI strategy, other than to note its command suggestions/autocomplete is quite good at guessing the next command I want to run.


Ultimately, I want to see terminals+shells become REPLs, like FANOS or the headless shell protocol, but that requires a level of cross-industry coordination bigger than any particular shell/terminal.

comments.author: andyc
comments.text:
Well, we can always add one more layer of indirection, right?


I am not sure about that; I still stand by the analysis here: https://lobste.rs/s/ntruuu/lobsters_interview_with_matklad#c_zxcqky


I think the lock-in to Unix PTYs is especially bad and hard because there are 3 kinds of software involved (rather than 2, like many protocols):


The issue is that both the shell and the child processes write to the same PTY.

Let's suppose you can change the shell and the terminal, and that the authors coordinate.  What you can't change is the thousands and thousands of CLI tools that already exist.

So that is why FANOS uses the "clever" FD passing mechanism.  (which doesn't work on Windows -- even though Windows has terminals!   I would like to find a way to do that!)

So I am not sure another layer of indirection works.  bash and zsh start child processes directly, and they start them with the same stdin stdout stderr as the shell itself.


Although on the other hand, I guess HSP might try to wrap them, using a Warp-like shim.  And I argued for that at the time.

I think I conceded on  the ugly Warp-like PTY stream parsing, which FANOS does not have.

But I honestly don't remember now exactly how far HSP got.   We probably should have written something about that ... so the experiment wasn't "lost"

The full name


Sure -- but widely referred to at the time as Warp, or Warp N with a version number. The "Star Trek" reference was intentional but some lamebrain marketing lizard at IBM forgot to get permission to use the name before launch.
